anchor_text: so wan with care
summary: 'Wan' means pale, bloodless, sickly-looking. King Henry opens the play describing himself as physically drained by the civil wars that brought him to power — his careworn face is the outward sign of an inward guilt the play never lets him escape.
detail: The word comes from Old English 'wann' (dark, gloomy); by the early modern period it had narrowed to mean pale or pallid, especially the pallor of illness or exhaustion. Henry's first syllable in the play is a self-portrait of weakness, not triumph, framing the entire tetralogy's image of a king who seized the crown and found it gave him no rest. Compare 2 Henry IV 3.1: 'uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'wan' adj. sense 1: 'of a dark or dusky hue; gloomy, black'; by 15th c. mainly 'pale or sickly in hue.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1
OED s.v. 'wan' adj. accurately records sense 1 as 'dark, dusky, gloomy' (Old English) narrowing by the 15th c. to 'pale or sickly in hue'; the citation is a fair paraphrase of the real entry.
The gloss accurately reads 'wan' as pale/sickly and the interpretation that Henry's opening self-portrait frames a guilt-ridden reign is mainstream and well-supported by the play's arc.

anchor_text: breathe short-winded accents of new broils
summary: 'Accents' here means spoken words or utterances, not the way someone pronounces them. 'Broils' means armed conflicts or violent brawls. Henry says peace can only catch her breath long enough to speak briefly about new wars — wars he intends to fight abroad in the Holy Land.
detail: 'Accent' in the sense of 'speech, utterance' is common in Shakespeare (cf. Julius Caesar 1.3: 'an accent of the same'; Hamlet 1.5). 'Broil' (from Old French 'brouiller') was standard for both domestic tumults and battlefield fighting. The phrase 'short-winded' — winded like a sprinter who cannot catch his breath — images peace as gasping, barely alive.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'accent' (sense 2): 'language, words, speech'; s.v. 'broil': 'tumult, confused fighting, battle.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'accent' and 'broil' are real entries with the senses cited; both words and their senses are well attested in standard lexicography.
Both 'accents' as utterances and 'broils' as armed conflicts are standard Elizabethan senses, and the personification of peace as breathless is plainly in the text.

anchor_text: thirsty entrance of this soil / Shall daub her lips with her own children's blood
summary: Henry personifies England as a mother who has been drinking her own children's blood — a deliberately revolting image for the civil wars of his own seizure of power. 'Thirsty entrance' means the thirsting mouth or opening of the ground (soil opening to swallow blood, like a thirsty creature). This is England as a cannibal mother, not a nurturing one.
detail: The extended personification of England as a woman (with lips, children, fields) runs from TLN 5 through TLN 16 and is a set-piece of Elizabethan high political rhetoric, familiar from Richard II and the histories generally. 'Entrance' here means the opening or mouth (from Latin 'intrare' via Old French 'entree'), used for a gap or opening in the ground. 'Daub' (to smear with something thick) makes the image visceral — blood is not spilt but plastered onto the mother's lips. The technique of personifying the nation as a violated or suffering mother goes back to Gower and Lydgate.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'entrance': 'an opening, mouth' (citing this passage).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the civil wars of Richard II's deposition as the context for Henry's guilt-speech.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 5

Onions does gloss 'entrance' as 'an opening, mouth' citing early modern usage, and Holinshed (1587) is the acknowledged source for the civil-war context Henry describes; both citations are real and supportive.
Reading 'entrance' as the mouth or opening of the earth (soil drinking blood) is the standard editorial gloss, and the cannibal-mother personification is present from TLN 5-16 in the text.

anchor_text: trenching war channel her fields
summary: 'Trenching' means cutting deeply, slashing, gouging — from the digging of military trenches. The image is of war ploughing England's farmland not with ploughshares but with swords and boots, turning fields into scarred ditches.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'trench' v. sense 2: 'to cut, gash'; 'trenching' as verbal adj.: 'that cuts or digs deeply,' attested from 1590s.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 7
OED s.v. 'trench' v. and the verbal adjective 'trenching' in the sense 'cutting, gashing deeply' are real entries attested from the 1590s, consistent with the annotation's claim.

The sense of 'trenching' as deeply cutting or gouging (not yet exclusively the military-engineering sense) is well attested, and the agricultural-destruction image is coherent with the surrounding passage.

anchor_text: intestine shock / And furious close of civil butchery
summary: 'Intestine' means internal, within the same body — the same root as 'intestines,' the organs inside the body. 'Intestine war' or 'intestine shock' is a standard Elizabethan phrase for civil war, the kind that tears a nation apart from the inside. 'Close' means hand-to-hand grappling, physical contact in combat.
detail: The Latin 'intestinus' ('internal') was applied in classical Latin to civil conflict; Shakespeare's audience would hear both senses — the clinical anatomical word and the political one — giving the passage a slightly nauseating physical edge, as if the body politic is literally tearing out its own bowels. 'Furious close' (from 'to close' = to grapple in combat) pictures the moment soldiers grip each other with bare hands. Together the phrase makes civil war feel like self-surgery.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'intestine' adj. sense 2: 'internal; esp. of strife, broils: civil, domestic'; s.v. 'close' n. sense 5b: 'a coming to close quarters in fighting, a hand-to-hand encounter.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 12

OED s.v. 'intestine' adj. sense 2 ('internal; of strife: civil, domestic') and s.v. 'close' n. sense 5b ('hand-to-hand encounter in fighting') are real entries; the Latin etymology from 'intestinus' is correct.
Both senses — 'intestine' as internal/civil and 'close' as hand-to-hand grappling — are standard; the dual register (anatomical + political) is a recognized feature of the passage.

anchor_text: The edge of war, like an ill-sheathed knife, / No more shall cut his master
summary: A simile comparing civil war to a knife that is badly sheathed — the blade left partially exposed so it cuts the hand of the person carrying it. Henry says England has been slashing itself with its own weapon. The image neatly converts the abstract idea of civil war into a tangible household accident.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'ill-sheathed': cited as 'badly put in the scabbard, with the edge showing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 17

The Onions Shakespeare Glossary does not contain a standalone entry for 'ill-sheathed'; it is a compound adjective that Onions may note in passing rather than as a head-entry, and the precise citation 'badly put in the scabbard, with the edge showing' cannot be confirmed from available sources.
The simile is explicit in the text and the gloss — a poorly sheathed knife cutting its bearer — correctly identifies the vehicle and tenor without over-elaborating.

anchor_text: sepulchre of Christ-- / Whose soldier now, under whose blessed cross / We are impressed and engaged to fight
summary: Henry announces a crusade to the Holy Land — specifically to Jerusalem, where Christ's tomb (the Holy Sepulchre, the site of the crucifixion and burial) stood. He claims to be Christ's soldier, bound by a vow to fight the 'pagans' (Muslims) for control of Jerusalem. This vow was sworn at the end of Richard II and is a main political thread of the Henry IV plays.
detail: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem had been the supreme goal of Christian crusading since the First Crusade (1099). Henry's vow to crusade was his way of paying a public penance for the murder of Richard II — going to Jerusalem was understood as an act of expiation. Holinshed records the vow. In the event Henry never managed to go, dying with the plan still unfulfilled; a prophecy would later tell him he would die in 'Jerusalem' — which turns out to be a room in Westminster Palace (2 Henry IV 4.5). 'Impressed' means conscripted, pressed into military service. 'Engaged' means bound by a formal pledge.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), under Henry IV: records the King's vow to undertake a crusade to the Holy Land.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 19

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record Henry IV's crusade plans and the Jerusalem prophecy; the annotation's claim that Holinshed 'records the vow' is supported by the Internet Shakespeare Editions Holinshed text for 1H4.
The crusade-as-penance reading is standard across editors (Humphreys, Bevington, Weis); the 'Jerusalem' prophecy echo in 2H4 is correctly flagged as a consequent thread.

anchor_text: bootless 'tis to tell you we will go
summary: 'Bootless' means useless, pointless, without profit or result — nothing to do with footwear. Henry says it would be a waste of breath to repeat the crusade plan they already know about. The word comes from 'boot' in an older sense of 'benefit or profit' (as in 'to boot' = in addition, on top of the bargain).

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'bootless': 'unavailing, unprofitable, useless.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 28
Onions s.v. 'bootless' ('unavailing, unprofitable, useless') is a real entry and the etymology from 'boot' (profit, benefit) is standard and correct.
The etymology (from 'boot' = profit/benefit, not footwear) and the gloss 'useless, pointless' are correct and uncontroversial.

anchor_text: forwarding this dear expedience
summary: 'Expedience' (or 'expediency') here means an urgent enterprise or pressing matter — specifically the crusade. 'Dear' means important, weighty, of great concern (not expensive). Henry asks what his council decided about pressing forward with the crusade plan.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'expedience': 'haste, speed; an urgent affair'; s.v. 'dear': 'important, weighty' (sense distinct from 'costly').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 32
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'expedience' (haste, speed; urgent affair) and s.v. 'dear' (important, weighty) are real entries with the senses cited; both are standard Shakespearean usage.
'Dear' as weighty/important and 'expedience' as urgent enterprise are well-attested Elizabethan senses and the context supports them straightforwardly.

anchor_text: when, all athwart, there came
summary: 'Athwart' means across, cutting across the path — originally a sailing term for something crossing the line of travel at right angles, and so used for anything that obstructs or interrupts a plan. The news from Wales crossed ('came athwart') the council's plans like a rope thrown across a ship's course.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'athwart' adv./prep. sense 1: 'across the path of, in opposition to'; nautical sense from 15th c.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 35

OED s.v. 'athwart' adv./prep. records the senses 'across the path of, in opposition to' with earliest evidence from c. 1470 (late 15th c.); the nautical origin and obstructive sense are correctly stated.
The nautical origin and meaning 'across the path, obstructing' is accurate and the metaphor of news cutting across the council's plans fits the text precisely.

anchor_text: irregular and wild Glendower
summary: Owen Glendower (Owain Glyn Dwr) was a Welsh nobleman who led a major rebellion against Henry IV beginning in 1400. 'Irregular' was the royal government's term for rebels and outlaws who operated outside lawful military command — guerrilla fighters who refused to stand and meet in open battle. Holinshed is the principal English source for Glendower.
detail: Owain Glyn Dwr claimed descent from the native princes of Wales and in 1400 proclaimed himself Prince of Wales. His rebellion was the most serious challenge to Henry's authority in the early part of his reign, lasting until about 1415. Holinshed calls him 'a dangerous and presumptuous rebel,' emphasising his irregular, hit-and-run methods. In the play Glendower is given a rich, literary, even mystical character (he claims supernatural powers) that complicates the royal court's dismissal of him as merely 'wild.' The detail about Welsh women mutilating the English dead (TLN 42-45) is from Holinshed and was a stock atrocity narrative used to frame the Welsh as savage.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): account of Owain Glyn Dwr's rebellion, 1400-1415.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 39

Holinshed (1587) does account for Owain Glyn Dwr's rebellion from 1400 onward; the date 1400 for the start of the revolt and the rebellion lasting until c. 1415 are historically accurate and Holinshed is the principal English source.

The historical identification and the technical sense of 'irregular' as operating outside lawful military command are defensible; noting Glendower's later theatrical complexity is appropriate without overreaching.

anchor_text: such beastly, shameless transformation, / By those Welshwomen done, as may not be / Without much shame re-told
summary: Westmoreland alludes to Holinshed's report that Welsh women mutilated and sexually humiliated the corpses of English soldiers killed in battle — cutting off noses, ears, and genitals. Because the mutilation was sexual in nature Shakespeare declines to describe it on stage, using the circumlocution 'such misuse / as may not be / Without much shame re-told.' The moment codes the Welsh enemy as barbaric and outside the rules of civilised warfare.
detail: Holinshed (Chronicles, 1587) records of the battle at Bryn Glas (1402): 'The dead bodies of the Englishmen [were] shamefully intreated by the Welshwomen, cutting off their privities and putting them in their mouths, and thrust their noses between their buttocks.' The report is likely atrocity propaganda — no independent source corroborates it — but Holinshed prints it and Shakespeare follows, though he stays deliberately vague. Westmoreland's embarrassed circumlocution ('shameless transformation,' 'may not be without much shame re-told') is itself a rhetorical device: it announces the horror while declining to give its specifics, leaving the audience to infer the worst. This is the play's first introduction of Wales as a space of gendered threat, preparing for Glendower's later complexity.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): account of the battle at Bryn Glas and the treatment of English dead by Welsh women.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 43

Holinshed (1587) does record the Welsh women's mutilation of English dead at Bryn Glas in explicit terms, as confirmed by the Internet Shakespeare Editions Holinshed text; the annotation's paraphrase is accurate.

The gloss correctly identifies the Holinshed source, the sexual nature of the mutilation, and Westmoreland's deliberate rhetorical circumlocution; labelling the report as likely atrocity propaganda (no independent corroboration) is a sound scholarly caveat.

anchor_text: On Holy-rood day the gallant Hotspur there
summary: Holy Rood Day — the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross — fell on 14 September. It commemorated the discovery and return of the True Cross (the cross on which Christ was crucified) to Jerusalem. 'Rood' is an Old English word for cross. The Battle of Homildon Hill (spelled 'Holmedon' here), where Hotspur defeated the Scots under the Earl of Douglas, took place on that date in 1402.
detail: The date 14 September (Holy Cross Day) had a particular resonance: it was the same feast that commemorated the Emperor Heraclius returning the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629, and so it had overtones of Christian military triumph. The real battle — Homildon Hill, Northumberland, 14 September 1402 — was a notable English victory in which the English archers under the Earl of March and the Percys routed a large Scottish army. Shakespeare uses Holinshed's account closely, though he conflates and slightly distorts the sequence of events for dramatic purposes.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the battle of Homildon Hill, 14 September 1402 (Holy Rood Day).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 51

Holinshed confirms the battle of Homildon Hill ('Holmedon') on 'the Rood Day in harvest' (14 September 1402); the feast's commemoration of the True Cross's return to Jerusalem is a matter of standard liturgical record, and the date is confirmed.

Holy Rood Day as 14 September, the historical battle of Homildon Hill in 1402, and the connection to the Exaltation of the Cross feast are all accurate; the Heraclius gloss is defensible tradition, not overreach.

anchor_text: The Earl of Douglas is discomfited
summary: 'Discomfited' means defeated and thrown into disorder — a military term for a routed army that has lost cohesion, not simply lost a battle. It does not mean merely 'made uncomfortable,' which is the modern meaning. The Earl of Douglas (Archibald, 4th Earl of Douglas) was taken prisoner by Hotspur at Homildon Hill in 1402.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'discomfit' v. sense 1: 'to defeat in battle, to rout'; cf. 'discomfiture': 'utter defeat, rout' — distinct from modern 'discomfort.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 66

OED s.v. 'discomfit' v. sense 1 ('to defeat in battle, to rout') is a real entry distinguishing it from modern 'discomfort'; the historical fact that Douglas was taken prisoner at Homildon Hill is confirmed by Holinshed.
Distinguishing the military sense 'routed, thrown into disorder' from the modern weakened sense 'made uncomfortable' is correct and important for student readers.

anchor_text: Balk'd in their own blood
summary: 'Balk'd' (or 'balked') means piled up in ridges or heaps, like the 'balks' — the unploughed ridges left between furrows in a field. The image is of dead Scottish soldiers lying in heaps, like the unturned strips of earth a ploughman leaves. It is a deliberately agricultural metaphor applied to mass death.
detail: A 'balk' was the strip of unploughed land left between two furrows as a boundary marker in open-field strip farming. To say the dead are 'balk'd' is to see the battlefield as a grotesque field, the corpses as its harvest-ridges. The word could also mean 'checked, thwarted' (from Old Norse 'balkr,' a beam or bar), but here the primary meaning is the agricultural one of heaping or ridging, reinforced by the visual image of rows of fallen men.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'balk': 'a ridge between two furrows; hence, to heap up in such ridges' — citing this passage.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 68

Onions s.v. 'balk' as a ridge between furrows and the meaning 'to heap in such ridges' is a real entry, confirmed by OED s.v. 'balk' n., and multiple sources attest this passage as the primary Shakespearean example.

The agricultural 'ridge-between-furrows' reading is one editorial tradition (Onions, Wilson), but the equally prominent rival sense 'heaped up, checked/thwarted' is also well attested (OED sense 5), and the claim that the agricultural image is primary over the simple 'heaped' meaning is contested enough to warrant caution.

anchor_text: sweet Fortune's minion and her pride
summary: Fortune here is the classical goddess Fortuna, imagined as a woman who turns a great wheel of fate — raising some to the top and casting others down, capriciously. A 'minion' is a favourite, a beloved pet. Henry describes Hotspur as Fortune's darling, her prize exhibit. The compliment also carries a warning: what Fortune favours, she can just as quickly discard.
detail: The image of Fortune and her wheel derives from Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (6th century), which was the standard source in medieval and Renaissance thought for the concept of Fortune as an arbitrary, turning wheel. Being Fortune's 'minion' was double-edged: a favourite today could be Fortune's cast-off tomorrow. Henry's envy of Northumberland for having such a son is sharp — but the play will show Hotspur destroyed by this same reckless, fortune-dependent courage.

sources.name: Boethius
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (Fortune turning her wheel, the fickleness of earthly favourites).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 81

Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 is the correct locus for Fortune's wheel and her raising and casting down of earthly favourites; the source is real and directly supports the annotation's claim.

Fortune as Fortuna with her wheel, the Boethian heritage, and 'minion' as favourite/darling are all accurate; the ironic foreshadowing that Fortune's favourite falls is standard and warranted by the play's outcome.

anchor_text: riot and dishonour stain the brow / Of my young Harry
summary: 'Riot' in this period meant dissolute, wasteful living — drunkenness, debauchery, spending recklessly in the company of lowlifes. It is not the modern sense of a street disturbance. Henry is comparing Hotspur's military honour against Prince Hal's life of drinking, gambling, and keeping bad company in the Eastcheap taverns — which was known to everyone at court.
detail: The biblical parable of the Prodigal Son uses the same vocabulary: the younger son wasted his inheritance in 'riotous living' (Luke 15:13, Geneva Bible). The juxtaposition here — the honour-mad Hotspur versus the riot-stained Hal — is the play's central dramatic irony, since Hal is in fact performing riot as a calculated strategy for his eventual redemption. 'Stain the brow' continues the personification of shame as a physical mark on the face.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'riot' n. sense 3: 'wanton, loose, or wasteful living; debauchery, dissipation, extravagance.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 83

OED s.v. 'riot' n. sense 3 ('wanton, wasteful living; debauchery') is a real entry, and Geneva Bible Luke 15:13 does use 'riotous living' for the Prodigal Son's dissipation; both citations are accurate.

The archaic sense of 'riot' as dissolute living (not street disturbance) is correct, and connecting it to the Prodigal Son vocabulary without asserting Henry is directly alluding to the parable is appropriately measured.

anchor_text: some night-tripping fairy had exchanged / In cradle-clothes our children where they lay
summary: Henry imagines that a fairy swapped his son in the cradle with Hotspur -- the folk belief that fairies stole human babies and left fairy children ('changelings') in their place. Henry is saying: if only Hotspur were his son and Hal were a Percy. 'Night-tripping' means dancing or moving lightly through the night.
detail: The changeling belief was widespread in early modern England: fairies were said to covet beautiful human children, substituting sickly, strange, or misbehaving fairy children instead. The substituted child -- the changeling -- typically refused to thrive, ate little, cried constantly, and failed to develop properly. Henry's wish is pointed: Hal's dissolute behaviour makes him look like exactly the kind of defective substitution the folk tradition described. The same changeling motif is central to the Titania-Oberon quarrel in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

sources.name: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft
sources.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), on popular fairy belief, including fairies said to steal and substitute children.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 85

Rescued in 2026-06-01 review sweep — Dropped the wrong chapter locus (Bk IV ch.10 is on Robin Goodfellow) and generalized the Scot citation to the work; the changeling belief is robustly attested and the gloss is sound.

The changeling folk belief is accurately described and is the plain sense of the passage; noting the same motif in A Midsummer Night's Dream is a legitimate parallel without overreaching the annotation.

anchor_text: Malevolent to you in all aspects; / Which makes him prune himself
summary: 'Aspects' carries its astrological meaning: the angles at which planets align with each other and with a person's horoscope were called 'aspects,' and a malevolent aspect meant a hostile planetary alignment. Westmoreland is saying Worcester's hostility to the King is not occasional but total — every angle of his nature, every planetary sign of his character, points against Henry. 'Prune' means to preen, to dress one's feathers as a bird does — Hotspur is bristling and preening under Worcester's bad influence.
detail: In Elizabethan astrology the aspects — conjunction, opposition, trine, square, sextile — determined whether planetary influences were friendly or hostile; 'malevolent aspects' was a technical astro-medical phrase. Westmoreland accuses Worcester of being constitutionally, astrologically against the King in every way. 'Prune' (to trim the feathers, from Old French 'poindre') used of a person means to preen arrogantly — to ruffle up and dress oneself like a bird displaying. 'Bristle up / The crest of youth' extends the bird/animal metaphor: Hotspur erects his plumage or hackles.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'aspect' n. sense 5: 'the relative positions of the planets as they appear to an observer on earth; in astrology, the angular distance between two heavenly bodies'; s.v. 'prune' v. sense 2: 'of a bird: to trim the feathers with the beak; applied to persons: to dress oneself, trim.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 95

OED s.v. 'aspect' n. sense 5 (astrological angular positions of planets) and s.v. 'prune' v. sense 2 (of a bird, to trim feathers; applied to persons, to preen) are real entries with the senses cited.

The astrological sense of 'aspects' and 'prune' as preening (not pruning vegetation) are both correct; the claim that 'malevolent to you in all aspects' covers every astrological angle is a defensible intensifying reading supported by the context.

anchor_text: drinking of old sack
summary: 'Sack' was a sweet, fortified white wine imported from Spain or the Canaries — the Elizabethan equivalent of sherry. 'Old sack' simply means well-aged, well-drunk stock: Hal uses it to paint a picture of Falstaff as a man who does nothing but eat, drink, and sleep.
detail: The word 'sack' appears to derive from the French sac (dry), though the wine itself was anything but dry by modern standards — it was typically sweet and strong, around 15-17% alcohol. Falstaff is so closely associated with sack throughout the play that Poins nicknames him 'Sir John Sack-and-sugar' (TLN 200). In Henry IV Part 2 Falstaff delivers a famous mock-encomium on sherry-sack as the source of all wit and valor.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sack, n.4': 'A general name for a class of white wines formerly imported from Spain and the Canaries.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 108
OED s.v. 'sack, n.4' is a real entry; the quoted definition matches standard lexicographic usage for the Spanish/Canary wine.

The gloss is accurate: sack was a fortified Spanish/Canary white wine, 'old sack' simply means aged stock, and the characterisation of Falstaff as someone defined by drink is squarely supported by the text.

anchor_text: fair hot wench in flame-coloured taffeta
summary: Taffeta was a shiny silk fabric; 'flame-coloured' (orange-red) was associated with London prostitutes in the period, making the phrase a coded insult. Hal is saying the only sun Falstaff cares about would be a sexually available woman dressed in a prostitute's colours.
detail: Flame-colour (a bright yellowish-orange) was so strongly associated with women of low repute that the colour itself carried the implication without further explanation. Taffeta's sheen amplified the flashiness. The joke in Hal's speech is cumulative: he replaces all the proper markers of time (hours, minutes, the sun) with Falstaff's actual priorities (drinks, food, women).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'taffeta': used of showy or showy-dressed persons; flame-colour associated with loose women.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 113
Rescued in 2026-06-01 review sweep — Dropped the unverifiable Hentzner citation; kept Onions (which the source judge accepted) and softened summary from 'standard dress' to 'associated with.'

The association of flame-colour with women of low repute is well attested in Elizabethan period sources and the reading fits the line's comic logic of substituting Falstaff's real priorities for proper markers of time.

anchor_text: so superfluous to demand the time
summary: 'Superfluous' here means 'going beyond what is appropriate or useful' — it is pointless or impertinent of you. Hal is saying there is no reason for Falstaff to care about the hour of day given how he spends his time.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'superfluous': 'exceeding what is necessary; needless, uncalled for.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 115
Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'superfluous' exists and supports the gloss of 'needless, uncalled for'.
'Superfluous' as 'going beyond what is appropriate or needless' is the standard period sense and fits the syntax ('so superfluous to demand') without over-reading.

anchor_text: not by Phoebus,--he, that wandering knight so fair
summary: Phoebus (literally 'the bright one') is an epithet for Apollo, the Greek and Roman god of the sun. Falstaff means that thieves operate by night and moonlight, not by the sun. The parenthetical 'wandering knight so fair' seems to quote or parody a ballad about the sun-god, as if Falstaff half-remembers a line of romantic verse.

anchor_text: 'tis my vocation, Hal; 'tis no sin for a man to labour in his vocation
summary: Falstaff is parodying the Protestant doctrine of vocation — the Reformation teaching (drawn from 1 Corinthians) that every person has a God-given calling or occupation, and that honest labour in that calling is holy. anchor_text: if men were to be saved by merit, what hole in Hell were hot enough for him

His joke thus has two layers: on the surface, a comic condemnation of Gadshill; underneath, a knowing reference to the Reformation debate that shaped the audience's world.

anchor_text: pilgrims gong to Canterbury with rich offerings
summary: The road from London to Canterbury via Gad's Hill was the main pilgrimage route to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral — the most celebrated English pilgrimage destination, made famous by Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (c. 1387). anchor_text: the foolish Mortimer; Who, on my soul, hath wilfully betray'd
summary: Henry's refusal to ransom Edmund Mortimer is political, not personal: Mortimer had been proclaimed by Richard II as heir to the throne. If Henry ransomed and freed him, he would be releasing his own rival claimant. The king brands Mortimer a traitor and his marriage to Glendower's daughter a sign of treachery — but the audience also hears Hotspur's counter-case that Mortimer was simply captured in battle.

Holinshed makes the same conflation. For the play's purposes what matters is that Henry regards anyone connected to the Mortimer claim as a threat to his usurped crown. His insistence that Mortimer 'wilfully betrayed' his men is unprovable and probably dishonest; Hotspur's rebuttal (the 'gentle Severn's sedgy bank' passage) is more convincing dramatically.

anchor_text: great magician, damn'd Glendower
summary: Owen Glendower (Owain Glyndwr in Welsh) was the Welsh rebel leader who led a serious uprising against Henry IV from 1400 onwards. 'Magician' reflects his historical reputation — and his own self-presentation — as someone with supernatural powers; he claimed the stars foretold his greatness and could 'call spirits from the vasty deep.' Henry IV's 'damn'd' is purely hostile name-calling.

He had been educated in England as a lawyer at the Inns of Court, had served the English crown, and turned rebel in a land dispute in 1400; by 1404 he controlled most of Wales and entered into treaty with France. His reputation for magic and prophecy was cultivated deliberately: Holinshed reports that the heavens were disturbed at his birth, and the Welsh bardic tradition associated him with the prophecies of Merlin. Shakespeare develops all this in the following act (3.1).

anchor_text: Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog, and that is the next way to give poor jades the bots
summary: 'Dank' means damp and cold — feed left wet in a badly kept stable. 'Jades' are worn-out, poor-quality horses. 'The bots' are the larvae of a botfly (Gasterophilus) that infest a horse's stomach, causing serious illness; in the period the term covered several worm-infestations of horses. The Second Carrier's point is that the inn has deteriorated so badly since Robin Ostler died — the stable-floor is damp, the feed is sodden — that the horses will fall sick. This foreshadows the robbery: if Gadshill cannot get a lantern and get the horses out promptly, the whole operation risks failing before it begins.

anchor_text: by the Mass
summary: 'By the Mass' is an oath swearing by the Catholic Mass — the central rite of the Roman Catholic Church in which bread and wine are consecrated as the body and blood of Christ. Such oaths were extremely common in everyday speech in England before the Reformation and persisted long afterward in colloquial use. For ordinary working men like the carriers, it was an unremarkable exclamation, not a theological statement.

The carriers in this scene — lower-class working men, likely Catholic by background or at least indifferent to doctrinal distinctions — use such oaths naturally. The play's commoners and tavern world are marked throughout by pre-Reformation Catholic oaths ('by the Mass,' ''Odsbody,' 'by'r lady'), while noblemen tend to more restrained or secular language.

anchor_text: 'Odsbody
summary: 'Odsbody!' is a minced oath — a politely softened version of 'God's body,' swearing by the physical body of Christ. Minced oaths shortened or garbled the divine name to avoid the sin of blasphemy. The exclamation signals sharp frustration.
detail: An Act of Parliament in 1606 prohibited the profane use of God's name on stage; theatrical texts from before 1606 often preserve unminced forms, while later printings and revisions substitute softened versions. 'Odsbody,' 'Gadzooks' (God's hooks, i.e. the nails of the Cross), and similar oaths are a feature of Elizabethan comic speech across all social levels. The First Carrier is annoyed that his turkeys — livestock he is transporting — are starving while the lazy ostler fails to appear.

anchor_text: At hand, quoth pick-purse
summary: The Chamberlain sarcastically quotes a proverb: 'At hand, quoth pick-purse' — meaning that thieves are always conveniently nearby when there is something to steal. Gadshill, calling 'What, ho! chamberlain!', gets back a response that knowingly labels both of them as thieves before a word of business has been spoken. The Chamberlain is showing Gadshill that he understands exactly what kind of 'hand' is being called for.
detail: The proverb 'At hand, quoth pick-purse' is recorded in collections of Elizabethan proverbial sayings. It mocks the pickpocket's eagerness — always 'at hand,' always ready. Gadshill's comeback (TLN 637-639) twists the joke back: the chamberlain of an inn, who 'lays the plot' for thieves by passing on information about wealthy guests, differs from a common pickpocket only in method, not in character. Gadshill draws the analogy between giving direction (management) and labouring (actual theft): both are parts of the same crime. The exchange instantly establishes the Chamberlain as Gadshill's accomplice.

anchor_text: a franklin in the wild of Kent hath brought three hundred marks with him in gold
summary: A 'franklin' was a free landowner below the rank of gentleman -- prosperous but not titled, the substantial country farmer class. 'The wild of Kent' (the Weald) was a large forested region in the interior of Kent, between the North and South Downs. 'Three hundred marks' was a significant sum: a mark was two-thirds of a pound, so 300 marks = 200 pounds, roughly a comfortable craftsman's income for two decades.
detail: Franklins appear in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales as solid, hospitable landowners who traveled with cash. The Weald of Kent was one of England's major wool and iron-producing regions, so a franklin traveling from there to London with gold was carrying the proceeds of rural commerce. The Chamberlain's tip follows a recognizable pattern in Elizabethan 'rogue literature' -- the inn servant who tips off highwaymen about wealthy guests. The phrase 'it holds current' (TLN 640) means the intelligence is still reliable, using a monetary metaphor (current coin) that suits a scene about money.

anchor_text: if they meet not with Saint Nicholas' clerks, I'll give thee this neck
summary: 'Saint Nicholas' clerks' was thieves' cant for highwaymen and robbers. Saint Nicholas is the patron saint of travelers and also of thieves — two interests that naturally collide on the road. Calling robbers his 'clerks' (servants) was a dark joke already current in Elizabethan rogue literature. Gadshill is saying the travellers will certainly be robbed. The Chamberlain's reply that Gadshill 'worshippest Saint Nicholas as truly as a man of falsehood may' confirms that Gadshill is himself one of the saint's 'clerks.'
detail: Saint Nicholas's patronage of thieves derives from medieval legend and may relate to stories of his miraculous rescues of the condemned; by the Elizabethan period 'Saint Nicholas' clerks' was established cant recorded in rogue pamphlets. John Awdeley's The Fraternity of Vagabonds (1561) and Thomas Harman's Caveat for Common Cursitors (1566) — the two main Elizabethan rogue books — catalogue the terminology and hierarchy of the criminal underworld. Gadshill's boast that he runs with 'nobility and tranquillity' (TLN 660) not mere foot-pad ruffians is a self-conscious claim to gentlemanly crime.

anchor_text: there are other Trojans that thou dreamest not of, the which, for sport-sake, are content to do the profession some grace
summary: 'Trojans' here is Elizabethan slang for boon companions, rogues, or good fellows — not a reference to the ancient city of Troy. Gadshill's boast that his associates are so powerful that if things went wrong they could 'make all whole' (TLN 657-658) — i.e. cover up the crime — is a clear hint to the audience that Prince Hal is involved, even as it keeps the secret from the Chamberlain. The joke that royalty is doing highway robbery 'for sport-sake' is the play's most pointed comic irony in this scene.

anchor_text: no foot land-rakers, no long-staff sixpenny strikers, none of these mad mustachio purple-hued malt-worms
summary: Gadshill is boasting that his associates are not low-grade ruffians. 'Foot land-rakers' are vagabond thieves who work on foot, picking pockets or snatching purses in fields and lanes — the lowest class of petty criminal. 'Long-staff sixpenny strikers' are robbers who use a quarterstaff to knock down victims for small change. 'Mad mustachio purple-hued malt-worms' are drunken, mustachioed tavern-sots — men whose faces have gone red from drinking cheap ale (malt liquor).

'Malt-worms' (devoted drinkers of ale, worms in a malt-tub) appears in other contexts as a term of contempt. Gadshill is making a social distinction: his gang is at the quality end of the criminal world — 'nobility and tranquillity, burgomasters and great oneyers' (TLN 660-661) — a comic claim that highwaymen can have class distinctions just like honest society. anchor_text: they pray continually to their saint, the Commonwealth; or, rather, not pray to her, but prey on her, for they ride up and down on her, and make her their boots
summary: Gadshill builds a sustained pun: his noble associates 'pray' to the Commonwealth as their patron saint, then corrects himself — they do not pray to her but 'prey' on her (the words were pronounced alike in Elizabethan English). 'Make her their boots' means use her as a profit, a 'booty' — but 'boots' also means riding boots, so they 'ride up and down on her' like a horse while wearing her as their footwear. The Commonwealth — the common wealth, the public good — is simultaneously worshipped, hunted, and ridden.
detail: The pun 'pray/prey' is a figure called antanaclasis — the repetition of a word in a different sense. The Chamberlain then picks up the 'boots' image literally ('will she hold out water in foul way?' TLN 666-667 — asking if she is like a good waterproof boot), and Gadshill responds by extending it ('justice hath liquor'd her,' TLN 668 — greased her leather with a waterproofing fat). The joke is politically pointed: those in power ('nobility and tranquillity') exploit the commonwealth as freely as highway thieves, but with greater impunity. The joke glances at a real Elizabethan anxiety about corruption in high places.

anchor_text: we have the receipt of fernseed,--we walk invisible
summary: Fern-seed was a piece of Elizabethan folk magic: ferns reproduce by spores so tiny they were invisible to the naked eye, and popular belief held that carrying fern-seed gathered on Midsummer Eve would make the bearer invisible. Gadshill is joking that since his powerful associates would suppress any investigation, the gang effectively operates unseen — as if they had this magical seed. The Chamberlain punctures the joke at TLN 671-672: they are really invisible only because they operate at night.
detail: The belief in the magical properties of fern-seed was widespread in England and recorded by Reginald Scot in The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), who debunks it. The invisibility of fern-seeds comes from the observation that ferns seem to reproduce without visible seeds — before the understanding of spores. The joke is also a preview of the robbery scene: Hal and Poins, working at night in disguise, really will achieve a kind of practical invisibility (2.2-2.4). The idea of walking invisible recurs in Henry V, where the king walks disguised among his troops before Agincourt.

anchor_text: Go to; homo is a common name to all men
summary: Gadshill ends with a mock-learned quip from Latin grammar: 'homo' (the Latin word for 'man' or 'human being') is a 'common noun,' applicable to every person regardless of rank — so both a 'true man' (an honest person) and a 'false thief' are, technically, human beings and 'homo' applies to both. The joke simultaneously dismisses the Chamberlain's word-game about 'true man' versus 'false thief' (TLN 673-675) and shows off a scrap of schoolboy Latin.

Gadshill has just promised his cut of the 'purchase' (loot) while calling himself 'a true man' (TLN 673-674) — a phrase that in English means 'honest' but which he is now dissolving into Latin so it means nothing. The bit of schoolroom Latin from a highwayman is itself a joke about the social range of the gang: these are educated rogues.

anchor_text: frets like a gumm'd velvet
summary: To 'fret' means both to chafe irritably and to wear away by rubbing. 'Gummed velvet' is velvet stiffened with gum arabic to make it hold its nap, a practice that made the fabric fray and crumble faster under friction. Poins is saying Falstaff is rubbing himself raw with impatience — just like cheap, treated cloth that falls apart under stress.
detail: Gum arabic was routinely applied to velvet and other luxury fabrics to make them appear fuller and retain their texture in the shop window; the treatment was known to shorten the fabric's life, since the stiffened pile cracked and shed under wear. The comparison is nicely double-edged: Falstaff is being compared to something that looks richer and more durable than it actually is.

anchor_text: I am not John of Gaunt, your grandfather; but yet no coward
summary: John of Gaunt (1340-1399) was the Duke of Lancaster, third surviving son of Edward III, and grandfather to Prince Hal. His name was commonly taken to mean 'John the thin' (from Ghent, his birthplace, pronounced to sound like 'gaunt'), making him a figure associated with lean hardiness. Falstaff's joke is a pun: Hal has just called him 'Sir John Paunch,' so Falstaff deflects by saying he may not be a gaunt (lean) hero like the royal grandfather, but he is no coward either. anchor_text: I must speak in passion, and I will do it in King Cambyses' vein
summary: King Cambyses was the hero of a popular early Elizabethan play (c. 1560) by Thomas Preston, famous for its ranting, bombastic style of tragic speech. Henry is voicing the Elizabethan theological principle that usurpers invite providential retribution — God uses the children of the guilty to punish the parents. The speech draws on a chain of guilt that began when Henry deposed Richard II and had him killed.

The gloss that 'doom' means divine judgment or decree is etymologically sound, textually supported (Henry is voicing providential guilt over the deposition of Richard II), and entirely mainstream in Shakespeare scholarship.

anchor_text: the hot vengeance and the rod of Heaven
summary: The 'rod of Heaven' is God's instrument of punishment — the biblical image of a rod or scourge God sends to chastise the wicked. Henry fears Prince Hal has been appointed by God as this punishing rod, sent to afflict Henry for his usurpation of Richard II.
detail: The image draws on multiple biblical passages in which God sends a foreign power or sinful instrument to punish his people. The clearest parallel is Isaiah 10:5: 'O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger' (Geneva 1599), where God uses a heathen king as his scourging tool. The word 'scourge' three lines earlier (TLN 1610) reinforces this: a scourge is a whip of punishment. Henry's logic is theologically precise — he is not saying Hal is wicked in an absolute sense, but that God employs even the wayward as an instrument of providential retribution.

The 'rod of Heaven' as God's punishing instrument, with Isaiah 10:5 as the parallel, is a well-established biblical image and the reading is fully consistent with the scene's providential theology; the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: smiling pick-thanks and base news-mongers
summary: A 'pick-thank' is a flatterer or informer — someone who curries favor by carrying tales to a superior. 'News-mongers' are gossips or rumor-peddlers. Prince Hal argues that many of the stories reaching the King about his wayward behavior come from self-serving courtiers trying to ingratiate themselves by reporting — and embellishing — bad news about the prince.
detail: The compound 'pick-thanks' is derived from 'picking' (seeking or picking up) and 'thanks' — one who seeks gratitude by tale-bearing and flattery. Nashe and other Elizabethan writers use it as a term of contempt for parasitic courtiers. The two words together set up a picture of the court as an environment where gossip is currency, a context relevant to Hal's broader argument that the King has been manipulated by malicious reports.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1627

Both 'pick-thanks' (tale-bearing flatterers) and 'news-mongers' (gossip-peddlers) are accurately defined, and the reading that Hal is blaming courtly informers for embellishing reports to the King is precisely what the text says — a defensible, mainstream gloss.

anchor_text: So common-hackney'd in the eyes of men, / So stale and cheap to vulgar company
summary: 'Hackney'd' means hired out, worn out by common use — from the hackney horse, a horse let out for hire to anyone. 'Vulgar' means common or ordinary people, not shameful (its modern sense). Henry is saying that Richard II made himself as cheap and available as a hired horse, overexposed to ordinary crowds, which destroyed the mystique of royalty.
detail: A hackney was a type of horse let for hire, hence something overused and devalued. The word transferred to any person or thing made cheap by overuse. Henry's argument is a calculated theory of political theatre: kings must ration their public appearances to preserve awe. This contrasts sharply with his own demagogic behavior later in this same speech, where he describes 'stealing' courtesy and allegiance from men's hearts — Henry's account of his own past is not entirely honest.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'hackney,' adj. sense 2: 'Let out for hire; hence, common, much used, ordinary.' First cited usage c. 1600.

'Hackney'd' from the hired horse meaning worn out by common use, and 'vulgar' as 'common people' rather than shameful, are both standard Elizabethan senses; the note that Henry's account of his own past is not entirely honest is a sound critical observation supported by the speech itself.

anchor_text: like a comet, I was wonder'd at
summary: Comets were regarded in Elizabethan England as extraordinary signs in the heavens, portending great events — war, plague, the death of kings. Henry says that his rare public appearances made him a wonder like a comet: people stopped and pointed. The image also carries an undercurrent of dread, since comets were ominous.
detail: The Elizabethan belief that comets signified catastrophe came from classical sources (e.g., Virgil, Georgics 1.488, and Pliny, Natural History 2.23, both on comets as portents of disaster) and was reinforced by repeated experience of comets appearing before major upheavals. Calphurnia in Julius Caesar (2.2) catalogues comets among the omens before Caesar's death. Henry's comparison of himself to a comet implicitly frames his rise to power as an event of cosmic scale — and, unconsciously, as a portent of the violent upheaval that followed.

sources.name: Pliny
sources.citation: Pliny, Natural History 2.23 (comets as portents of civil war and the deaths of princes).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): comets regularly cited as signs preceding the deaths of kings and nobles.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1650

Pliny Natural History 2.23 is confirmed to discuss comets as portents of civil war and political upheaval (including the civil disorder of 87 BC and the wars of Pompey and Caesar); Holinshed's use of comets as omens is well-attested as Shakespeare's source context.

The reading that comets were Elizabethan portents of catastrophe and that Henry compares his rare appearances to such wonders is sound; the added observation that comets carried ominous undertones (implicitly framing his rise as catastrophe) is a defensible interpretive suggestion rather than an overreach, given that the play itself frames Henry's usurpation as the source of ongoing disorder.

anchor_text: I stole all courtesy from Heaven, / And dress'd myself in such humility, / That I did pluck allegiance from men's hearts
summary: Henry says he 'stole' courtesy from Heaven — meaning he borrowed or assumed the condescending grace of a monarch chosen by God. He performed humility so convincingly that he won the people's love away from the reigning King Richard II. The word 'stole' is revealing: Henry admits the divine sanction was not rightfully his.
detail: The passage is Henry's most candid self-analysis in the play. He acknowledges that his popularity was a performance, a strategy. 'Courtesy from Heaven' invokes the doctrine of divine right — God's favor was supposed to inhere in the anointed king, not be appropriated by a usurper. The irony runs through the whole speech: Henry condemns Prince Hal for exactly the casual familiarity with the crowds that Henry himself once used to displace Richard II.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Bolingbroke's conspicuous popularity with the common people during his return from exile, before seizing the crown.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1653

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) is the confirmed primary source for the history plays and does describe Bolingbroke's strategic popularity and his campaign that unseated Richard II, supporting the annotation's historical claim.

The reading that 'stole courtesy from Heaven' signals Henry's self-aware acknowledgment that the divine sanction was not rightfully his — and the irony that he condemns Hal for the same populist behavior he himself used — is a mainstream critical position firmly grounded in the text.

anchor_text: like a robe pontifical, / Ne'er seen but wonder'd at
summary: A 'robe pontifical' is the ceremonial vestment of a bishop or pope ('pontiff'), brought out only for the most solemn occasions. Henry compares his carefully rationed royal presence to a bishop's most magnificent robes — items so rarely displayed that they are always objects of awe whenever they appear.
detail: 'Pontifical' derives from Latin 'pontifex,' a high priest, and refers specifically to garments reserved for the most solemn liturgical ceremonies of a bishop. The comparison quietly lifts Henry's political image-management into a quasi-religious register: his presence is a kind of sacrament, rare and therefore sacred. The analogy is also slightly ironic given that Henry broke from established order to seize the crown.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pontifical,' adj. sense 1: 'of or pertaining to a pontiff, bishop, or pope; befitting a bishop; characterized by the dignity or authority of a bishop.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1659

OED s.v. 'pontifical' adj. sense 1 ('of or pertaining to a pontiff, bishop, or pope; befitting a bishop') is a genuine entry that directly supports the annotation's explanation of the word's meaning and register.

A 'robe pontifical' as the ceremonial vestment of a bishop reserved for solemn occasions is correctly defined, and the comparison to Henry's rationed royal presence is a sound reading; the observation that the analogy is 'slightly ironic' is defensible but stated cautiously enough not to overreach.

anchor_text: The skipping King, he ambled up and down / With shallow jesters and rash bavin wits, / Soon kindled and soon burnt; carded his state
summary: The 'skipping King' is Richard II, Henry's predecessor and the king he deposed. 'Bavin wits' are people as flimsy and quick-burning as bavin — bundles of small brushwood used only to kindle a fire. 'Carded his state' means he adulterated or degraded his royal dignity, as a cloth-maker cards (combs) wool by mixing in inferior fibers.
detail: Richard II's taste for favorites and court entertainers was a standard item in Tudor historical writing about him. Holinshed describes Richard 'haunting the company of riotous persons' and spending 'large gifts amongst parasites and flatterers.' The image of bavin — light, quick-burning brushwood kindling — is a precise metaphor for superficial wits whose cleverness is bright but instantly consumed. 'Card' as a verb meaning to adulterate or debase comes from the cloth trade: unscrupulous dealers would card inferior wool into a fine fleece. Henry is painting Richard's court as a degraded, fraudulent version of true majesty.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Richard II's prodigality toward flatterers and parasites.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bavin': 'Bundle of brushwood; faggot of small twigs or light pieces of wood used for kindling fire.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1663

Holinshed's account of Richard II's association with favorites and prodigal behavior is well-attested as Shakespeare's source; OED s.v. 'bavin' ('bundle of brushwood; faggot of small twigs used for kindling') is genuine and directly supports the metaphor described.

'Bavin wits' as light quick-burning brushwood and 'carded his state' as adulterating royal dignity from the cloth trade are both accurate, standard glosses; the historical identification of the 'skipping King' as Richard II and the Holinshed source for his favourites are uncontroversial.

anchor_text: Enfeoff'd himself to popularity
summary: To 'enfeoff' (pronounced 'in-FEF') is a legal term from the feudal land system: to give someone possession of land with all its rights and obligations. Henry says Richard made himself the permanent property of the common crowd — surrendered his royal independence to the mob as absolutely as a lord grants land to a vassal.
detail: In feudal law, to enfeoff was to formally invest a person with a fief (a grant of land in exchange for service). The word was still in legal use in Shakespeare's time. The metaphor is startling: kings grant fiefs — they do not give themselves as fiefs. Richard, by ingratiating himself with the populace, has reversed the proper hierarchy of feudal obligation, placing himself in servitude to popularity. Henry makes this point to illustrate why Hal's similar behavior is a loss of royal dignity.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'enfeoff,' sense 1: 'To invest with a fief or fee; to put in legal possession of a freehold.'

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'enfeoff': 'to invest with a fee; to surrender (to anyone).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1672

OED s.v. 'enfeoff' sense 1 ('to invest with a fief or fee; to put in legal possession of a freehold') and Schmidt s.v. 'enfeoff' are genuine entries that directly support the feudal-legal meaning claimed.

The legal-feudal meaning of 'enfeoff' — to invest with a fief — is correct, and the reading that Richard has reversed the proper hierarchy by surrendering himself to the crowd as if he were the vassal is a sound and well-recognized interpretation.

anchor_text: They surfeited with honey, and began / To loathe the taste of sweetness, whereof a little / More than a little is by much too much
summary: Henry uses the saying that too much of a sweet thing turns to disgust, then tightens it into a paradox: 'a little / More than a little is by much too much.' The final line is a deliberate rhetorical turn -- an epigram or sententia (a terse, memorable saying) meant to stamp the lesson in memory. Excess destroys not just satisfaction but the taste itself.
detail: The sententia -- a brief, pointed moral observation -- was a standard tool of Elizabethan rhetoric taught in grammar schools. The honey-surfeit idea ('too much honey cloys the stomach') was proverbial. Shakespeare's version has an extra structural wrinkle: 'a little / More than a little is by much too much' turns on itself, quantifying the infinitesimally small trigger of excess. The rhetorical figure is correctio (self-correction, sharpening a statement to a finer point). The argument applies both to Richard's popular excess and, implicitly, to Hal's tavern indulgences.

anchor_text: he was but as the cuckoo is in June, / Heard, not regarded; seen, but with such eyes / As, sick and blunted with community
summary: The cuckoo calls loudly and distinctively in spring (April-May), when it arrives from Africa, and is greeted with delight as a sign of the season; by June it is still calling, but people have stopped noticing. Henry uses it to describe how Richard's constant presence made people tune him out the way they tune out a familiar bird-call. 'Community' here means familiarity, over-exposure.
detail: The cuckoo was proverbially associated with May Day and spring in English culture; its call was a welcome herald (compare 'When daisies pied... the cuckoo mocks married men' in Love's Labour's Lost 5.2). By summer the cuckoo's call has become part of the background. Henry's comparison makes a precise social-psychological point: the human capacity for wonder is diminished by repetition. 'Blunted with community' — dulled by over-familiarity — captures exactly what he is warning Hal against.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1678

The cuckoo-in-June comparison is a documented Elizabethan proverbial idea, but the specific Tilley entry number C901 could not be verified; the annotation's prose claim is plausible but the precise citation reference cannot be confirmed.

The cultural gloss that the cuckoo is welcomed in spring but ignored by June is accurate, the reference to Love's Labour's Lost provides apt intertextual support, and 'community' as over-familiarity is the standard Shakespearean sense; no overreach.

anchor_text: from France set foot at Ravenspurg
summary: Ravenspurgh (modern Spurn Head, Yorkshire) was the landing point on the north-east coast of England where Henry Bolingbroke came ashore in July 1399 after his exile in France, to begin the campaign that ended with his seizing the crown from Richard II. Henry is recalling the moment his usurpation began.
detail: Holinshed names Ravenspur as the landing place of Bolingbroke's return from exile in the summer of 1399. The historical landing at Ravenspur — a spit of land near the mouth of the Humber — is dramatized in Richard II (Act 2). At the time of this scene in Henry IV Part 1, the landing is only about four years in the past, and Henry is using it as a pointed comparison: Hal is now what Richard was then — an unregarded, overexposed figure who has lost the people's attention.

sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Bolingbroke lands at Ravenspur (Ravenspurgh), July 1399, with a small force.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1699

The historical identification and Holinshed sourcing are sound, but the reference card linked is 'the-great-chain-of-being' — which has no clear relevance to a place-name annotation about Ravenspur; the annotation body itself is defensible, but the reference card link is a mismatch that may indicate a copy-paste error rather than an interpretive overreach.

anchor_text: this Hotspur, Mars in swathing-clothes, / This infant warrior
summary: Mars was the Roman god of war -- the most feared and honored of battlefield deities. 'Swathing-clothes' are swaddling bands used to wrap a newborn infant tightly. Henry is calling Hotspur 'Mars still in his cradle': a war-god not yet fully grown but already terrifying. The hyperbole sets up the contrast with Prince Hal, who despite his age is doing nothing martial at all.
detail: The conceit of a heroic figure being compared to a young, potent deity is a recognized form of heroic compliment in classical rhetoric (syncrisis, or comparison). Henry's point is that Hotspur -- described in the play as about the same age as Hal -- has already won extraordinary martial renown. The phrase also carries a slight undercutting edge: Mars in baby-clothes is almost absurd, which is why Henry needs both 'Mars' for the god-like martial quality and 'infant warrior' to stress that Hotspur achieves this while still young.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses

anchor_text: Capitulate against us, and are up
summary: 'Capitulate' here does not mean 'surrender' (its modern meaning). In Elizabethan usage it means to draw up or agree to terms and articles — to form a formal covenant or league. The rebels have signed a compact of articles against the King and risen in arms ('are up').
detail: The word derives from Latin 'caput' (head) through 'capitulum' (chapter, article), hence 'capitulate' = to agree to terms by chapter. The modern sense of 'surrender' comes later and from a different branch of the same root (the terms of a capitulation). In this context, the line means that Percy, Northumberland, the Archbishop, Douglas, and Mortimer have formally combined by treaty and taken the field. The OED records the 'draw up articles' sense as current through the seventeenth century.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'capitulate,' sense 1 (obsolete): 'To draw up under heads or chapters; to treat upon articles; to make terms or conditions.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1724

OED s.v. 'capitulate' sense 1 (obsolete, 'to draw up under heads or chapters; to treat upon articles; to make terms or conditions') is a genuine entry that directly supports the archaic meaning distinguished from the modern 'surrender' sense.

The archaic sense of 'capitulate' as 'draw up articles / make a formal compact' (not 'surrender') is the correct Elizabethan meaning and is well-supported by the OED; the annotation accurately flags the false friend for modern readers.

anchor_text: Percy is but my factor, good my lord, / T' engross up glorious deeds on my behalf
summary: A 'factor' is a business agent who trades or collects goods on behalf of a principal employer. To 'engross' is to buy up wholesale, to accumulate in bulk. Prince Hal casts Hotspur as his commercial agent, stockpiling honor and glory that Hal will then claim by defeating him. The metaphor treats battlefield glory as a tradeable commodity.
detail: The commercial vocabulary (factor, engross) is deliberately mundane and ironic for such high martial subject matter — it is one of Hal's characteristic moves to deflate heroic inflation with mercantile language. 'Engross' in the sense of buying wholesale or accumulating appears in legal and commercial contexts (an 'engrosser' was someone who bought up goods to monopolize them, an offense under Tudor statutes). Hal's metaphor is both boast and wit: he is saying he has let Hotspur collect all the honor so that the eventual reckoning will be all the more spectacular.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'factor,' sense 4: 'An agent who transacts business for another; a commercial agent or broker.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'engross,' sense 2: 'To buy up wholesale; to acquire in large quantities with a view to monopoly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1751

OED s.v. 'factor' sense 4 ('an agent who transacts business for another; a commercial agent or broker') and OED s.v. 'engross' sense 2 ('to buy up wholesale; to acquire in large quantities with a view to monopoly') are genuine entries directly supporting both glosses.

The commercial metaphor of 'factor' (agent) and 'engross' (buy up wholesale) is accurately glossed, and the reading that Hal deliberately deflates heroic inflation with mercantile language — a characteristic Hal move — is a defensible, widely accepted critical observation.

anchor_text: the end of life cancels all bands
summary: 'Bands' are bonds — legal obligations, written contracts. To 'cancel' a bond was to cross it through or cut it (literally scoring the document). Hal is saying that if he fails to keep his vow, death will at least wipe out all debts and promises, since no obligations survive the grave.
detail: The word 'band' for a bond or legal contract was interchangeable with 'bond' in Elizabethan usage (both derive from the idea of binding). A band-cancelled is a discharged obligation. The legal metaphor fits into the speech's broader commercial and financial vocabulary: Hal has been talking about Percy as his 'factor,' about 'rendering' glories, and now about death as a final cancellation of accounts. The line also reflects the Elizabethan legal practice of cancelling an instrument of debt by scoring or cutting the document — 'cancelling' derives from Latin 'cancelli' (a lattice or cross-hatching).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'band,' sense 10: 'A written obligation; a bond, deed of covenant.' (Elizabethan legal usage.)

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'band': 'bond, fetter; a bond, a written obligation.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1761

OED s.v. 'band' sense 10 ('a written obligation; a bond, deed of covenant') and Schmidt s.v. 'band' ('bond, fetter; a written obligation') are genuine lexicographic entries that directly support the Elizabethan legal sense of 'bands' as bonds.

'Bands' as bonds or written obligations and 'cancel' from the practice of scoring a document are both standard Elizabethan legal usages, and the reading that Hal is using legal-commercial vocabulary to close his vow-speech is entirely sound and consistent with the surrounding language.

anchor_text: Advantage feeds him fat, while men delay
summary: Henry closes the scene with a sententious proverb: opportunity grows stronger while the cautious hesitate. 'Feeds him fat' means fattens the enemy's strength (as livestock are fattened for slaughter). This type of clinching maxim — a sententia — was standard for ending a scene, sending the audience away with a moral in mind.
detail: The sententia was a rhetorical device drawn from classical oratory and taught in Elizabethan grammar schools via Erasmus and Cicero; a speech or scene closed with a memorable general truth was considered well-finished. The image of delay as feeding the enemy echoes a military commonplace (cf. Caesar, Bellum Gallicum, on the cost of hesitation), and the personification of 'Advantage' as a creature being fattened gives the abstract warning vivid, physical force. The couplet structure (paired thought: 'while X, Y') follows the form of Latin sententiae.

Identifying the closing line as a sententia and the 'feeds him fat' image as a vivid personification of opportunity fattening the enemy is a sound reading; the Tilley reference is well-chosen for the proverbial context.

anchor_text: fallen away vilely since this last action
summary: 'Fallen away' means grown thin or wasted. 'This last action' is the Gad's Hill robbery and its aftermath. Falstaff opens the scene by claiming the excitement has wasted him to a shadow — a joke given that he is famously enormous.

'Action' in Elizabethan English could mean a military engagement or any vigorous deed; here it carries the sense of the Gad's Hill caper. anchor_text: I could wish this tavern were my drum
summary: A 'drum' was both the instrument beaten to call soldiers to muster and the military headquarters or meeting-place for a company. Falstaff wishes the Boar's Head tavern were his drum: he would rather assemble his troops (and conduct his 'wars') in the comfort of the tavern than march out in the field. The wish neatly summarises his entire relationship to soldiering.

anchor_text: soldier of this season's stamp / Should go so general-current
summary: Hotspur compares Douglas to a freshly minted coin: a soldier of 'this season's stamp' means one stamped or coined in this age, and 'general-current' means accepted as good currency everywhere, like a coin that passes freely through any market. The metaphor praises Douglas as a warrior whose valor is recognized throughout the world.

Editors gloss 'stamp' as the impression made by a die, confirming the coin imagery throughout.

anchor_text: I defy / The tongues of soothers

anchor_text: No man so potent breathes upon the ground / But I will beard him

anchor_text: Zwounds! how has he the leisure to be sick
summary: 'Zwounds' is a contracted oath from 'by God's wounds' — a reference to Christ's wounds on the cross. It was one of the most forceful oaths in Elizabethan English, somewhere between 'damn it' and a stronger modern expletive. Parliament's Act to Restrain Abuses of Players (1606) later banned oaths like this from the stage, which is why later editions sometimes soften it.

The oath was so common in Shakespeare's age that it had already weakened somewhat from genuine blasphemy to a strong exclamation; Hotspur uses it as a reflexive outburst of frustration. The 1606 Act drove many such oaths out of later quartos and folios of various plays.

anchor_text: set the exact wealth of all our states / All at one cast? to set so rich a main / On the nice hazard
summary: Hotspur uses gambling imagery to argue against committing everything on a single battle. 'Cast' is a single throw of the dice; a 'main' is the total stake put up at risk in the dice game hazard; 'nice hazard' means a perilously uncertain chance. He is asking: would we be wise to stake everything on one roll?
detail: Hazard was a popular Elizabethan dice game in which players called a 'main' (a number between 5 and 9) before throwing; the entire stake rode on whether that number came up. The extended gambling metaphor (cast, main, hazard) was a natural idiom for a military wager. The passage is often noted as an example of Hotspur's more reflective side — he is actually counselling caution here, not recklessness.

The gambling-imagery glosses (cast = dice throw, main = total stake, hazard = dice game) are standard and well-attested; the aside noting this shows Hotspur's reflective side is a defensible, mainstream critical reading of the passage.

anchor_text: remains a sweet reversion; / And we may boldly spend upon the hope / Of what is to come in
summary: A 'reversion' is a legal term for an estate or income that will come to the heir when the current holder dies — a future inheritance already promised but not yet received. Douglas is arguing that Northumberland's army, though absent now, is a guaranteed resource they can count on receiving later, like money one knows is coming and can spend in anticipation.
detail: The legal vocabulary of inheritance (reversion, come in) was familiar to Elizabethan audiences who dealt in entailed property. The conceit — spending now on the credit of a future reversion — also subtly acknowledges the rebels' precarious position: they are gambling on the expectation of reinforcements that have not arrived.

anchor_text: the Devil and mischance look big / Upon the maidenhead of our affairs
summary: 'Maidenhead' means the beginning or first phase of a venture — literally, 'the head (front) of the maiden (new, untested) enterprise.' In plain English: 'if things look bad at the very outset of our campaign.' The word also carried its literal meaning (virginity), adding a comic edge to Hotspur's phrase that the rebels' enterprise is still untested and vulnerable.
detail: The double sense was deliberate and conventional: 'maidenhead' appears in Elizabethan writing as both 'first attempt' and 'virginity,' and the context ('look big' = appear threatening, menacing) reinforces the latent image of something looming over an untouched venture. The pun fits Hotspur's characteristic tendency to mix bravado with inadvertent comedy.

anchor_text: The quality and hair of our attempt / Brooks no division
summary: 'Hair' here means nature or character — what something is made of, its grain or texture (as in the 'hair' of a piece of wood). 'Quality and hair' together mean the nature and temper of the enterprise. 'Brooks no division' means will not tolerate, cannot endure, any splitting of the rebel forces. Worcester is warning that their rebellion is too delicate an enterprise to survive the appearance of internal fracture.

summary: The 'offering side' means the party that issued the challenge — the rebels, who are the aggressors in this conflict. Worcester is saying: as the side that provoked this war, they cannot afford any crack through which hostile, impartial eyes might examine their motives.

summary: 'Make a head' is a military idiom meaning to raise and muster an army, to bring one's forces to a fighting strength sufficient for a campaign. Hotspur is arguing that if the rebels can press on without Northumberland's forces and still threaten the Crown, their strength will seem all the more formidable when Northumberland's army joins them.

anchor_text: All plumed like estridges that with the wind / Bate it
summary: 'Estridges' are ostriches (a variant spelling, from Spanish avestruz via Old French). To 'bate' means to beat the wings impatiently and struggle to take flight — a term from falconry for a hawk that flaps and strains against the leash. Vernon is painting the Welsh and English knights in their plumed helmets as a flock of great birds straining and beating their wings as the wind hits them, restless to be loosed.
detail: Editors have also proposed 'estridges' = goshawks (a separate bird used in hawking), which would make the falconry meaning of 'bate' more consistent; but the ostrich reading is supported by the specific word form and by the visual of massive plumes tossing in the wind. Either way, 'bate' is unambiguously a falconry term for the hawk's frustrated wing-beating. Vernon's entire speech (TLN 2049-2062) is a sustained blazon of the royal army's splendor.

anchor_text: young Harry--with his beaver on, / His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd
summary: A 'beaver' is the movable face-guard of a helmet — the hinged visor that can be raised or lowered; here it is down, meaning the Prince is battle-ready and his face is hidden. 'Cuisses' (pronounced 'KWIS-iz') are the armor plates that protect the thighs. Vernon is describing Prince Hal fully armed for war from head to leg, a sharp visual contrast to the idle tavern-haunter Hotspur expects.

anchor_text: Rise from the ground like feather'd Mercury, / And vault it with such ease into his seat
summary: Mercury (Greek Hermes) was the messenger of the gods, famous for the small wings attached to his heels and his helmet that let him fly across the sky at supernatural speed. Vernon compares Prince Hal vaulting onto his warhorse to Mercury launching himself from the earth — effortless, weightless, otherworldly. The image transforms Hal from tavern-wastrel into something divine.
detail: The 'feathered Mercury' figure was a stock image of swift, graceful action in Elizabethan poetry (compare Marlowe's Tamburlaine and Spenser's Faerie Queene). The immediate source is Ovid's Metamorphoses, where Mercury travels on winged heels (talaria) and a winged hat (petasus). Vernon's speech as a whole (TLN 2049-2062) is the play's most sustained praise of Hal, and its source in pagan mythology deliberately elevates the Prince to near-divine status in Hotspur's enemy camp — making Hotspur's rivalry with him all the more significant.
